resources.title: Semantics derived automatically from language corpora contain human-like biases
resources.abstract: Machines learn what people know implicitly AlphaGo has demonstrated that a machine can learn how to do things that people spend many years of concentrated study learning, and it can rapidly learn how to do them better than any human can. Caliskan et al. now show that machines can learn word associations from written texts and that these associations mirror those learned by humans, as measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT) (see the Perspective by Greenwald). Why does this matter? Because the IAT has predictive value in uncovering the association between concepts, such as pleasantness and flowers or unpleasantness and insects. It can also tease out attitudes and beliefs—for example, associations between female names and family or male names and career. Such biases may not be expressed explicitly, yet they can prove influential in behavior. Science , this issue p. 183 ; see also p. 133

resources.title: Bias Measurement — WEFE user guide
Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings
resources.abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. We define metrics to quantify both direct and indirect gender biases in embeddings, and develop algorithms to "debias" the embedding. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

resources.title: Word embeddings quantify 100 years of gender and ethnic stereotypes
resources.abstract: Significance Word embeddings are a popular machine-learning method that represents each English word by a vector, such that the geometry between these vectors captures semantic relations between the corresponding words. We demonstrate that word embeddings can be used as a powerful tool to quantify historical trends and social change. As specific applications, we develop metrics based on word embeddings to characterize how gender stereotypes and attitudes toward ethnic minorities in the United States evolved during the 20th and 21st centuries starting from 1910. Our framework opens up a fruitful intersection between machine learning and quantitative social science.

resources.title: Image Representations Learned With Unsupervised Pre-Training Contain Human-like Biases
resources.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning leverage massive datasets of unlabeled images from the web to learn general-purpose image representations for tasks from image classification to face recognition. But do unsupervised computer vision models automatically learn implicit patterns and embed social biases that could have harmful downstream effects? We develop a novel method for quantifying biased associations between representations of social concepts and attributes in images. We find that state-of-the-art unsupervised models trained on ImageNet, a popular benchmark image dataset curated from internet images, automatically learn racial, gender, and intersectional biases. We replicate 8 previously documented human biases from social psychology, from the innocuous, as with insects and flowers, to the potentially harmful, as with race and gender. Our results closely match three hypotheses about intersectional bias from social psychology. For the first time in unsupervised computer vision, we also quantify implicit human biases about weight, disabilities, and several ethnicities. When compared with statistical patterns in online image datasets, our findings suggest that machine learning models can automatically learn bias from the way people are stereotypically portrayed on the web.

sample_claims.text: The recommendation system's item embeddings do not cluster products along demographic lines in ways that limit cross-group exposure
The document retrieval system's embedding space geometry does not position certain demographic groups in disadvantaged regions affecting search relevance
The medical language model's clinical term embeddings maintain equitable distances across patient demographic attributes
The content moderation system's embedding space properties are documented including encoded sensitive attributes and their spatial relationships

techniques.name: Reward Hacking Detection
techniques.description: Reward hacking is when an agent trained to maximise a proxy reward (a score that only approximates what its designers want) raises that score by exploiting its gaps while the intended outcome stalls or worsens. Detection scores each trained policy (the agent's decision rule) on the proxy and on an independent measure of the intended objective that training never used, such as a true reward from a simulator, a held-out 'gold' reward model or human ratings. Repeating this at every saved training checkpoint and model size matters because the originating study found capability thresholds at which the true reward drops sharply while the proxy keeps rising. When the true objective cannot be scored in operation, the study instead flags a policy whose actions diverge too far from those of a trusted policy that people have already verified. The output is a pair of reward curves showing where they part, or an anomaly score for each candidate policy.

example_use_cases.description: A transport authority training a reinforcement-learning ramp-metering controller in a traffic simulator rewards it on mean vehicle speed, but also logs average commute time for all drivers at every checkpoint. Checkpoints where speed keeps improving while commute time worsens (for example by holding merging cars back indefinitely) are rejected before any field trial.

A team fine-tuning a customer-support language model with reinforcement learning from human feedback scores each checkpoint with its training reward model and with a held-out reward model and a sample of human ratings that the training loop never sees, and stops training at the point where the training reward keeps rising but the held-out scores fall.

Before an insulin-dosing agent trained against a simulator reward goes to clinical evaluation, the developers score every candidate policy on a separate true objective, time spent in the safe blood-glucose range, and exclude any policy whose simulator reward is high but whose time in range is lower than that of the clinically reviewed baseline policy.

A public-health modelling unit that replaces a reviewed epidemic-response policy with a larger retrained one compares the new policy's actions with the reviewed policy's across simulated outbreaks. A divergence score above the threshold set on earlier policies with known outcomes sends the new policy to expert review instead of adoption, because its true outcome cannot be scored before deployment.

limitations.description: Everything rests on the independent measure of the intended objective. When that measure is itself a proxy (a gold reward model, or a small sample of human ratings), a policy can exploit it too, and the comparison then only detects divergence between two imperfect measures. Collecting enough human ratings at every checkpoint is expensive, which is why studies substitute a gold reward model.

It detects gaming only along the dimensions the true measure scores. A policy that exploits something the true objective does not capture (a side effect, a safety constraint, a user group not represented in the ratings) passes the check, so a clean result is evidence about the measured objective only.

The trusted-policy detector is weak and inconsistent. In the originating benchmark every baseline detector scored an area under the ROC curve below 60% on at least one task, and no detector was best on all tasks, so a quiet detector is not evidence that hacking is absent.

The trusted-policy detector flags difference, not harm. It needs a policy that people have already verified, and comparable action distributions from both policies, and a candidate that is genuinely better than the trusted policy can diverge from it and be flagged, which makes false alarms likely when the trusted policy is only moderately good.

Because the onset of reward hacking can be abrupt as capability grows, checking a few checkpoints or one model size can miss it. The comparison has to be repeated at every checkpoint and model size that might be deployed, which multiplies evaluation cost, especially when the true measure needs human raters.

resources.title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
resources.abstract: Reward hacking -- where RL agents exploit gaps in misspecified reward functions -- has been widely observed, but not yet systematically studied. To understand how reward hacking arises, we construct four RL environments with misspecified rewards. We investigate reward hacking as a function of agent capabilities: model capacity, action space resolution, observation space noise, and training time. More capable agents often exploit reward misspecifications, achieving higher proxy reward and lower true reward than less capable agents. Moreover, we find instances of phase transitions: capability thresholds at which the agent's behavior qualitatively shifts, leading to a sharp decrease in the true reward. Such phase transitions pose challenges to monitoring the safety of ML systems. To address this, we propose an anomaly detection task for aberrant policies and offer several baseline detectors.

resources.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
resources.abstract: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart’s law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed “gold-standard” reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

techniques.name: Operating-Point ROC Analysis
techniques.description: Operating-point ROC analysis measures how often a classifier makes each kind of mistake at the decision threshold it will actually use, which is the evidence behind claims such as 'the false-positive rate stays within acceptable bounds'. A classifier that outputs a score is turned into a yes-or-no decision by a threshold, and moving the threshold trades one kind of error against the other. On a labelled held-out set, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true-positive rate (the share of actual positives that are flagged, also called sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged, equal to one minus specificity) at every possible threshold; the operating threshold is then chosen from the curve to meet a stated limit on one error rate or to minimise the expected cost of errors, or an existing threshold is confirmed. At that one threshold the analysis reports the confusion matrix (the counts of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives) and the false-positive and false-negative rates with their complements, specificity and sensitivity. The output is a set of error rates tied to a named threshold and a named test set, against which a requirement on error rates can be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team evaluating a vendor's sepsis alert scores a year of its own admissions, plots the ROC curve and fixes the alert threshold its operations committee chose from the vendor's recommended range. At that threshold it reports sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and the share of all admissions that would trigger an alert, and uses the false-positive count and alert volume to decide whether ward staff can act on the alerts.

A card-payments company re-runs the analysis every month on transactions its fraud analysts have labelled, confirms that the false-positive rate at the live threshold is still under the limit agreed with its customer-service team, and, whenever the rate has drifted above that limit, reopens the threshold choice on the latest ROC curve and confirms the new threshold on the following month's labelled sample.

A manufacturer's quality engineers choose the threshold for a visual-inspection model by weighing the cost of scrapping a good part against the cost of shipping a defective one, using the ROC curve and the line's defect rate, then report the false-reject and defect-escape rates that the chosen threshold gives on a separate held-out production batch.

A rail operator's safety team assessing a camera-based obstacle detector for level crossings sets the decision threshold on a tuning set so that the miss rate meets the requirement allocated to the detector. It then measures the false-negative rate at that threshold on a separate set of recorded crossings, broken down into daylight, night and rain, and enters the confusion matrices in the safety case as verification evidence.

limitations.description: The rates are evidence only if they are measured on labelled cases that played no part in choosing the threshold. A threshold set to give a 1 per cent false-positive rate on a tuning set gives exactly that rate there by construction, and with a few hundred negative tuning cases its true rate on new data can be half as high again. Choosing the threshold on one set and reporting rates on another, or nesting the choice inside cross-validation, avoids this at the cost of more labelled data.

False-positive and true-positive rates do not change with how common the positive class is, but the share of alerts that are correct does. A false-positive rate within its limit can still mean most alerts are false when the condition is rare: at 90 per cent sensitivity and a 5 per cent false-positive rate, only about 15 per cent of alerts are correct when 1 case in 100 is positive. Claims about alert burden need the positive predictive value at the deployment prevalence as well.

A rate from a finite test set is an estimate, and with few negatives or few errors it can fall well below the true rate by chance. A claim that a rate is within a limit needs a confidence interval (exact binomial for a single rate; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics for other metrics) narrower than the margin to the limit. With no misses, about 3,000 positives show a miss rate below 1 in 1,000, and 30,000 below 1 in 10,000, at 95 per cent confidence.

The threshold is a fixed score, so the rates hold only while the scores for each class stay as in the test set. A new scanner, fraud pattern or patient mix shifts the scores and moves the false-positive rate with no change to the model, so the analysis must be repeated on labelled operational samples, which can be slow or costly. Labels matter too: where only flagged cases are reviewed, the rate for unflagged cases is unknown unless a random sample of them is labelled.

A single rate averages over the whole test set. It can meet its limit overall while exceeding it for a group of people or an operating condition (night-time images, one hospital site) that is rare in the test data. Rates need reporting for each group and condition the claim covers, each with enough cases to be informative, which can multiply the labelled data required.

resources.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients
resources.abstract: Importance: The Epic Sepsis Model (ESM), a proprietary sepsis prediction model, is implemented at hundreds of US hospitals. The ESM's ability to identify patients with sepsis has not been adequately evaluated despite widespread use. Objective: To externally validate the ESM in the prediction of sepsis and evaluate its potential clinical value compared with usual care. Design, Setting, and Participants: This retrospective cohort study was conducted among 27 697 patients aged 18 years or older admitted to Michigan Medicine, the academic health system of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, with 38 455 hospitalizations between December 6, 2018, and October 20, 2019. Exposure: The ESM score, calculated every 15 minutes. Main Outcomes and Measures: Sepsis, as defined by a composite of (1) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance criteria and (2) International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision diagnostic codes accompanied by 2 systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria and 1 organ dysfunction criterion within 6 hours of one another. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve at the hospitalization level and with prediction horizons of 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours. Model calibration was evaluated with calibration plots. The potential clinical benefit associated with the ESM was assessed by evaluating the added benefit of the ESM score compared with contemporary clinical practice (based on timely administration of antibiotics). Alert fatigue was evaluated by comparing the clinical value of different alerting strategies. Results: We identified 27 697 patients who had 38 455 hospitalizations (21 904 women [57%]; median age, 56 years [interquartile range, 35-69 years]) meeting inclusion criteria, of whom sepsis occurred in 2552 (7%). The ESM had a hospitalization-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.62-0.64). The ESM identified 183 of 2552 patients with sepsis (7%) who did not receive timely administration of antibiotics, highlighting the low sensitivity of the ESM in comparison with contemporary clinical practice. The ESM also did not identify 1709 patients with sepsis (67%) despite generating alerts for an ESM score of 6 or higher for 6971 of all 38 455 hospitalized patients (18%), thus creating a large burden of alert fatigue. Conclusions and Relevance: This external validation cohort study suggests that the ESM has poor discrimination and calibration in predicting the onset of sepsis. The widespread adoption of the ESM despite its poor performance raises fundamental concerns about sepsis management on a national level.

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Reliability Diagram with Expected Calibration Error
techniques.description: A reliability diagram with expected calibration error (ECE) measures whether a classifier's stated confidence matches how often it is right, so that a reader can tell whether predictions given a probability of 70 per cent come true about 70 per cent of the time. Using labelled cases the model was not trained on, each prediction's confidence (the probability given to the predicted class, or to an event such as rain above a threshold) is placed in one of a fixed number of bins, commonly ten or fifteen equal-width intervals between 0 and 1, and in each bin the average confidence is compared with the observed frequency, the share of its cases in which the predicted class or event actually occurred. The reliability diagram plots observed frequency against average confidence bin by bin, so that bins below the diagonal show overconfidence and bins above it underconfidence, and is usually shown with a histogram of how many cases fall in each bin, which the diagram itself does not show; the ECE condenses the same comparison into one number, the average gap between confidence and observed frequency weighted by each bin's share of the cases, and the maximum calibration error reports the largest gap in any bin. The technique measures and changes nothing: Platt scaling, isotonic regression calibration and temperature scaling repair a model's probabilities, and this measurement, run before and after on the same held-out cases, none of them used to fit the repair, is the evidence that a repair worked.

example_use_cases.description: A national meteorological service is deciding whether to issue a neural-network nowcast's probabilities that radar reflectivity will exceed set thresholds within the next hour. On a held-out season of radar composites, its verification team draws reliability diagrams with sample-count histograms and computes the ECE for each threshold and lead time beside those of its current extrapolation ensemble, and issues the new probabilities only for thresholds where they are at least as reliable.

A hospital's imaging AI group receives a chest X-ray classifier whose vendor reports good calibration on public data. Before connecting it, the group computes the reliability diagram and ECE on a year of its own labelled studies, finds the model overconfident in its highest bins, fits temperature scaling on a separate validation split, and repeats the measurement on the untouched test split to show whether the gap has closed.

A law firm's knowledge team evaluating a language-model research assistant that reports a confidence with each answer asks it a held-out set of questions with verified answers, bins its self-reported confidence, and computes the reliability diagram and ECE for each practice area rather than only for the whole set. The confidence display is switched off for practice areas where the gap between stated confidence and accuracy exceeds the firm's threshold.

A card issuer's fraud team checks its transaction-risk model each month on transactions whose outcomes have arrived, using bins fixed at validation that are narrow over the high scores where alerts are raised. Because fraud is rare, nearly all cases fall in the lowest bin and dominate the ECE, so the team tracks the gap in each high-score bin as well; a gap above the limit set at model sign-off triggers an investigation of drift and a decision on recalibration.

limitations.description: The result depends on how predictions are binned. With equal-width bins, confident models put most cases in one or two bins, which dominate the ECE while the others rest on few cases; more bins give a finer measurement but a noisier estimate in each bin. Rankings of recalibration methods can change with the number of bins or the binning scheme, so both must be reported and held fixed in any comparison.

Binning distorts the estimate in both directions. Overconfident and underconfident predictions in the same bin cancel, so with plenty of data the binned ECE understates the true error. On small samples, sampling noise inflates it: with 15 equal-width bins, a simulated perfectly calibrated model showed large errors on 200 cases. ECEs from samples of different sizes, such as subgroups, are not directly comparable; equal-mass bins or a debiased estimator reduce the bias.

Calibration says nothing about how well the model separates cases. A model that gives every case the overall base rate, such as 0.5 on a balanced dataset, is calibrated but useless, so the ECE must be reported with accuracy, the area under the ROC curve or a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score, which combines calibration with how decisive the predictions are.

Weighting by bin size gives rare but important predictions almost no weight. In a precipitation nowcasting study, almost all probabilities for heavy-rain thresholds fell in the lowest bin, so the ECE barely registered the rare high-probability forecasts, and at the highest threshold it could not be compared because some bins were empty. For multi-class models the usual ECE also looks only at the top predicted class and ignores the calibration of the others.

The measurement holds only for the population and period it was computed on. One ECE over a whole test set can hide large differences between subgroups: in an evaluation of language models answering medical questions, ECE ranged from 0.041 to 0.141 across specialties, a spread the pooled figure masked. Calibration can also drift after deployment, so it has to be measured for the subgroups that matter and repeated on new labelled data.

On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

Calibration of Self-Reported Confidence and Accuracy of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
resources.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. Materials and Methods: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Results: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties (“Skin” best: 0.041; “Social & Preventive Medicine” worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. Discussion: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. Conclusion: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved “self-knowledge”, but uneven overconfidence persists.

sample_claims.text: On the held-out 2025 convective season, the nowcast's probabilities of exceeding 25 dBZ at 30-minute lead time have an expected calibration error below 0.01 over ten equal-width bins, no higher than that of the current extrapolation ensemble.

After temperature scaling, the chest X-ray classifier's expected calibration error on the hospital's untouched test split is below 0.03 with 15 equal-width bins, and no bin holding more than 2 per cent of studies shows a gap above five percentage points.
For each practice area with at least 300 evaluation questions, the research assistant's self-reported confidence has an expected calibration error below 0.08 against verified answers.

In every month of 2026, in each high-score bin fixed at model sign-off, the fraud model's average predicted probability was within two percentage points of the observed fraud rate among transactions with confirmed outcomes.

techniques.name: Deletion and Insertion Curves
techniques.description: Deletion and insertion curves test whether a feature-attribution explanation, such as a heatmap over an image or highlighted words in a text, puts first the input features the model actually relies on. For the deletion curve, the evaluator removes features in the order the explanation ranks them, most important first, replacing each with a neutral value such as zero, the dataset mean, random noise or a blurred copy, and records the model's score for the explained class after each step; a faithful ranking makes the score fall quickly, so a smaller area under the curve is better (equivalently, a larger area over it, the AOPC score Samek et al. report). The insertion curve runs the other way: it starts from an input with every feature removed or blurred, restores features in ranked order, and rewards a fast rise. For text, the same procedure is often reported as comprehensiveness (how far the predicted-class probability drops when the top-ranked words are deleted) and sufficiency (how far it drops when only those words are kept), either at one cut-off or averaged over cut-offs from the top 1% to the top 50% of words. Explanation methods are compared on the same model, inputs and replacement value, against a random ranking as a baseline, and the result shows how well the ranking tracks the model's behaviour, not whether the highlighted features make sense to a person.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's cardiology informatics team has a deep network that measures intervals and amplitudes from 12-lead ECGs and must choose which heatmap method to show cardiologists. It perturbs the highest-ranked sample points first, one per step, tracks the rise in measurement error over several thousand ECGs, and compares each method's area under the error curve with that of random heatmaps. Because expert preferences and the curves can disagree, it reports both before choosing.

A regulator's data team routes consumer complaints with a fine-tuned transformer classifier and wants to highlight for caseworkers the words behind each routing decision. Before choosing between two word-attribution methods, it computes comprehensiveness and sufficiency on a validation sample at the 1, 5, 10, 20 and 50% cut-offs and adopts a method only if it clearly beats randomly ranked words on both measures.

A rail operator's engineering team uses an image classifier to flag defects in track inspection photographs and wants heatmaps that point inspectors to the defect. It runs deletion with pixels set to a constant and insertion from a blurred image for three heatmap methods, then repeats the deletion run with a second replacement value, and adopts a method only if it ranks first under both.

limitations.description: Removing pixels or words produces inputs unlike anything the model was trained on, so part of the drop in score can be the model reacting to an unfamiliar input rather than to the loss of the information the explanation pointed to, and the shape of the removed region can itself carry class information. Results are least trustworthy when large parts of the input are removed; variants that retrain the model or fill removed pixels from their neighbours reduce the effect.

The score depends on how features are removed and in what order. On one image classifier, the best-ranked method changed when removed pixels were set to the dataset mean instead of random colours, removing the least relevant pixels first ranked the methods roughly in reverse of removing the most relevant first, and rankings varied from image to image. A comparison holds only for the stated replacement value, order, step size and fraction removed, and should be checked under a second replacement.

Only the order of the attribution scores counts, not their size, so explanations with very different magnitudes can receive the same score. Taking absolute values of signed attributions changes the order and hence the result. The curves cannot tell an explanation that ranks the right features but gives them misleading magnitudes from one that gets both right; that needs a measure that uses the attribution values.

The curves show whether the ranking tracks the model, not whether the explanation is useful or correct for the domain: a model that relies on a spurious cue receives a faithful explanation of that cue. In a study of ECG models, ECG experts' choice of the best heatmap method disagreed considerably with the perturbation ranking, so a good curve does not show that experts will find the explanation helpful.

Each curve needs one model evaluation per step, for every input and method compared, so fine-grained curves over large images, long documents or big test sets are expensive. In the original region-perturbation study, two settings over 5,040 images each, with 100 steps repeated ten times because the replacement values were random, took roughly 36 hours on a workstation with 20 hyper-threaded Xeon cores in 2015. Coarser steps cut the cost but make the curve less able to separate methods.

techniques.name: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
techniques.description: Sanity checks for saliency maps are two randomisation tests that show whether an explanation method's output depends on what a neural network has learned, or would look much the same for a network that had learned nothing. In the model parameter randomisation test, the evaluator recomputes explanations for a fixed set of inputs after replacing the trained weights with random ones, either cumulatively from the output layer down towards the input (cascading randomisation) or one layer at a time with the others left trained (independent randomisation). In the data randomisation test, the evaluator trains a copy of the same architecture on the training data with the labels shuffled, until it has memorised them, and compares its explanations with those of the model trained on the true labels. Similarity between original and randomised explanations is measured with rank correlation, with and without absolute values, and with image similarity scores such as the structural similarity index; a method whose maps stay similar fails, because its output cannot reflect the learned weights or the relationship between inputs and labels, as Guided Backpropagation and Guided GradCAM failed in the original study when the upper layers were randomised, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed. Passing is a necessary condition, not proof of a good explanation: it shows a method responds to the model, not that its explanations are faithful or useful.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology AI group considering saliency maps as a guide to where a chest-radiograph model sees a pneumothorax runs cascading randomisation on the trained network, measuring structural similarity between original and randomised maps after each block. It sets aside methods whose maps stay similar, as several common methods did in a published study of this task, unless a deletion test shows they still track the model, and uses the rest only alongside a separately validated localisation model.

An insurer's fraud analytics team shows investigators attribution scores for each claim flagged by a neural-network model. Before rollout it runs independent layer randomisation, one layer at a time, and checks that rank correlation without absolute values falls for every layer, so that the scores investigators see depend on the trained weights throughout the network rather than mostly on the claim's raw feature values.

A wind-farm operator's reliability team uses a one-dimensional convolutional network on gearbox vibration signals and gives maintenance engineers heatmaps over each signal. It runs the data randomisation test by training the same architecture on shuffled fault labels until it fits them, and keeps only heatmap methods whose maps differ clearly between the two networks, since a map that survives shuffled labels cannot show what the network learned about faults.

limitations.description: Passing is easy for an explanation that carries no information. Binder et al. show that attribution maps with no correlation between neighbouring pixels score well in model randomisation tests, and that top-down randomisation tends to preserve the scale of forward-pass activations, so even a good explanation can change only so much. They argue the test should not alone decide whether a method is kept: two methods that score poorly on it beat several gradient methods in occlusion-based tests.

The verdict depends on how similarity is measured. In the original study, rank correlation with absolute values and structural similarity stayed high for some methods after randomisation while rank correlation without absolute values fell to near zero, because randomisation flipped signs but kept the input's outline. There is no agreed pass threshold and libraries set their own defaults, so the measure, absolute-value setting and threshold must be reported with the result.

The similarity measures are sensitive to noise, so a method with noisy maps looks changed by randomisation partly because of its own noise, and its score is overstated. Later work proposes repairs: averaging each explanation over noisy copies of the input before comparing (Smooth MPRT), or comparing how much more complex the explanation becomes after full randomisation (Efficient MPRT); its authors report more reliable results with both.

The model parameter test needs the weights and a layered network, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an interface. The data randomisation test needs the training data and pipeline and a network able to memorise shuffled labels; the original study trained to over 95% training accuracy, which for a large model costs a full training run.

Most evidence for the tests comes from image classifiers. Passing says nothing about whether the highlighted regions match what matters in the domain: in a chest-radiograph study, every saliency method, including those that passed the randomisation test, localised abnormalities worse than a dedicated detection or segmentation network.

resources.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
resources.abstract:
Saliency methods have emerged as a popular tool to highlight features in an input
deemed relevant for the prediction of a learned model. Several saliency methods
have been proposed, often guided by visual appeal on image data. In this work, we
propose an actionable methodology to evaluate what kinds of explanations a given
method can and cannot provide. We find that reliance, solely, on visual assessment
can be misleading. Through extensive experiments we show that some existing
saliency methods are independent both of the model and of the data generating
process. Consequently, methods that fail the proposed tests are inadequate for
tasks that are sensitive to either data or model, such as, finding outliers in the data,
explaining the relationship between inputs and outputs that the model learned,
and debugging the model. We interpret our findings through an analogy with
edge detection in images, a technique that requires neither training data nor model.
Theory in the case of a linear model and a single-layer convolutional neural network
supports our experimental findings.

Assessing the Trustworthiness of Saliency Maps for Localizing                     Abnormalities in Medical Imaging
Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

sample_claims.text: Every saliency method used in the chest-radiograph review tool produced maps whose structural similarity to the original fell below the agreed threshold once the top blocks of the network were randomised, on a held-out sample of radiographs.

For the fraud model's attribution scores, rank correlation without absolute values between original and layer-randomised attributions is below the threshold set in the validation plan for every layer tested.

Heatmaps from the methods kept for the gearbox dashboard differ between the network trained on true fault labels and the same architecture trained on shuffled labels, by more than the threshold stated in the test report.

techniques.name: GNNExplainer
techniques.description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

resources.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
resources.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs.GNNs combine node feature information with the graph structure by 
recursively passing neural messages along edges of the input graph. However, incorporating both graph structure and feature information leads to complex models,
and explaining predictions made by GNNs remains unsolved. Here
we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. Given an instance, GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that have a crucial role in GNN's prediction. 
Further, GNNExplainer  can generate consistent and concise explanations for an entire class of instances.
We formulate GNNExplainer as an optimization task that maximizes the mutual information between a GNN's prediction and distribution of possible subgraph structures. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that our approach can identify important graph structures as well as node features, and outperforms baselines by 17.1% on average. GNNExplainer  provides a variety of benefits, from the ability to visualize semantically relevant structures to interpretability, to giving insights into errors of faulty GNNs.

techniques.name: TimeSHAP
techniques.description: TimeSHAP explains one prediction of a model that reads a sequence of events, such as a recurrent neural network that scores a bank transaction using the account's history, by giving each past event, each input feature and selected event-feature cells a Shapley value: a share of the score, taken from cooperative game theory, such that all the shares add up to the difference between the model's score and its score with every event and feature removed. It adapts KernelSHAP, the sampling estimator in SHAP, which explains a single input vector and so, applied to the latest event of a recurrent model, gives earlier events no credit; TimeSHAP instead switches off whole rows or columns of the event-by-feature input matrix, replacing them with a background value (the training-data average in the original paper), queries the model on many such perturbed sequences, and fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the attributions. Because the number of event combinations doubles with every event, a pruning step first walks back from the most recent event and merges all older events into a single player once their combined attribution falls below a chosen tolerance, and cell-level values are computed only where the most important events and features intersect, with the other cells grouped. The model is treated as a black box that takes a batch of sequences and returns one score per sequence, and the output is event, feature and cell attributions for each explained sequence, plus plots that aggregate them across many sequences into a global view.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's fraud operations team runs TimeSHAP on each alert from its recurrent account-takeover model, so the analyst reviewing an alert sees which earlier events (for example a password change, then a login from a new device) and which features carried the score, not only the payment being held. The analyst uses this to decide whether to release the payment or contact the customer, and the model team samples the explanations to check that the drivers match known fraud patterns.

A hospital data-science team validating a recurrent model that predicts next-day escalation of treatment for patients in intensive care computes event- and feature-level TimeSHAP values for test-set patients and reviews them with clinicians. Drivers the clinicians judge implausible, such as an indicator that a measurement is missing outweighing the measurements themselves, are investigated before the model is used in a prospective study.

An airport's forecasting team using a recurrent model to warn of fog in the next six hours from the past 48 hours of station observations uses the pruning statistics and global event plots to find how far back the model actually draws on, and the feature attributions to check that humidity, temperature and wind lead each warning. The findings set the input window for the next retraining and go into the model's validation report.

limitations.description: Every attribution is measured against the background chosen to stand for a removed event or feature, the training-data average in the original paper. A sequence containing averaged events may be unlike anything the model has seen, and another background gives other attributions; the original authors note that a feature scoring zero for every sequence may reflect the background rather than the model. Report the background with the results.

Exact values need every combination of events, which doubles with each event. On the original fraud data (median sequence about 138 events), exact values were possible for only 10% of sequences with 32,000 sampled combinations, and repeated runs disagreed (relative standard deviation 1.71 without pruning, 0.98 at the chosen tolerance). With tens of thousands of model calls per explanation, explaining every scored event in real time is impractical; the alerts people review are the usual scope.

Pruning trades detail on older events for speed and stability. All events before the cut-off share one attribution. The cut-off test compares the older block's net, signed attribution with a user-set tolerance, so by construction an early event that pushed the score up can pass unseen if others pushed it down; the original paper does not measure how often this happens. Results change with the tolerance, so fix it in advance and report it.

It explains one score per sequence: the reference implementation expects the model to return a single value for each sequence. A model with many outputs, such as a forecast for several lead times or locations, needs a separate run or a chosen summary for each. The attributions show what the model relies on, not causes in the world: in the original study a high attribution to customer age led to a bias audit, which was needed to establish the disparity.

Each event and feature receives one number, so an effect that arises only from a combination, such as a settings change followed by a login from a new device, is shared out among its parts: an analyst sees each part with some credit but cannot tell that they matter only together. Cell-level values are computed only where the top-ranked events and features intersect. A clinical study using the method found escalation effects hard to see and suggested interactions as the cause.

techniques.name: Predictive Parity and Calibration Within Groups
techniques.description: This test checks whether a model's output means the same for every group: among people who receive the same score or the same decision, the share who turn out to have the outcome (or its average, for an outcome such as a cost or a count of illnesses) should not depend on their group, a requirement the fairness literature calls sufficiency. For a model that outputs a risk score, cases with known outcomes are grouped into score bins and, for each group, the observed outcome rate in each bin is plotted against the score, giving one calibration curve per group (a score is calibrated when, of the cases scored 0.3, about 30 per cent have the outcome); calibration within groups (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan) holds when each group's curve matches the scores, and the weaker condition that the curves coincide holds when a given score corresponds to the same outcome rate in every group. For a yes/no decision the same comparison is made in the two cells of the decision: predictive parity (Chouldechova) holds when the positive predictive value, the share of people flagged positive who turn out positive, is equal across groups, and the negative predictive value can be compared in the same way for those not flagged. The two read-outs can disagree, because a score that means the same for every group can still give unequal positive predictive values at a threshold when the groups' scores are spread differently above it, so the test reports the read-out matching the output on which decisions are taken, with intervals and the gaps between groups. Where comparisons of error rates condition on the true outcome and ask whether people who turn out the same are treated the same, this test conditions on the model's output and asks whether people treated the same turn out the same; when the outcome is more common in one group, the two cannot both hold except in special cases.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team checks a deterioration-risk score before it is shown to ward staff. On a year of admissions with recorded outcomes it plots a calibration curve, with intervals, for each ethnic group and each sex, and approves the score for use with every patient only if, across the scores that trigger escalation, each group's curve stays within a band agreed with clinicians.

A lender's model validation team compares the repayment rate among approved applicants across age bands, using two years of outcomes, to check whether approval means the same for each band. Because a difference among the approved can come from how scores are spread above the cut-off rather than from a different bar for one band, it also compares the calibration curves of the underlying score before raising any finding with the credit risk committee.

A probation service assessing a supplier's reoffending-risk tool is shown evidence that its positive predictive value is equal across ethnic groups. Its analysts reproduce the figures on local data and set them beside the groups' false positive and false negative rates, which differ because reconviction rates differ, so that the oversight board chooses which criterion the tool will be held to with both sets of figures in front of it.

A health insurer auditing a score that selects members for a care-management programme checks twice whether the score means the same for every racial group: against next year's costs, the label the model was trained on, and against a measure of illness such as the number of active chronic conditions. A score calibrated for cost but not for illness, with one group sicker than another at the same score, would lead the insurer to retrain on a different label.

limitations.description: When the outcome is more common in one group, a score or decision that satisfies predictive parity cannot also give the groups both equal false positive and equal false negative rates, and calibration within groups cannot coexist with equal average scores for each group's positives and negatives except with perfect prediction or equal base rates (Chouldechova; Kleinberg et al.). Passing this test therefore means accepting unequal error rates, a choice the test informs but cannot make.

Passing says little about how accurately the model predicts for each group. A well-fitted model usually comes close to calibration within groups without any fairness intervention when group membership can be inferred from its inputs, and a model that predicts accurately for one group while giving everyone in another group that group's average rate is still perfectly calibrated (Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan). The result needs pairing with performance measured for each group.

The test uses recorded outcomes, so it inherits any difference between groups in how the outcome is recorded. Rearrest stands in for reoffending, and a care-management score was calibrated by race for health costs while, at the 97th percentile of the score, Black patients had 26 per cent more chronic illnesses than white patients (Obermeyer et al.). A model can pass while scoring one group's need too low, so the outcome tested must be the one the claim is about.

A gap in positive predictive value is not by itself evidence that the score treats groups differently: the value averages over everyone above the threshold, so it depends on how each group's scores are spread there and moves when the threshold moves. Chouldechova notes that well-calibrated scores can fail predictive parity, and the converse also holds. Where scores are available the calibration curves should be reported, and the threshold stated.

Per-group calibration curves need labelled cases across the score range in every group; in a small group the high-score bins may hold a handful of people, so their rates swing widely, and the choice of bin widths changes the picture. An outside auditor who sees only decisions, not scores, can test predictive parity but not calibration, so access determines which claim the evidence can support.

resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.
